title: Gambler’s Fallacy
description: The belief that past independent random events affect the probability of future random events. After a streak, we think the opposite outcome is “due.”
shortDescription: The belief that past independent random events affect the probability of future random events. After a streak, we think the opposite outcome is “due.”

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The belief that past independent random events affect the probability of future random events. After a streak, we think the opposite outcome is “due.”

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A roulette player sees red come up six times and bets heavily on black because “it has to hit black soon.”
A hiring manager has rejected five candidates and thinks “the next one is bound to be good,” as if rejections increase future quality.
In a sales team, after a string of lost deals, the manager says “our luck is about to turn.” The coin has no memory.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Believing in “hot hands” and “cold streaks” in purely random events.
Making predictions based on perceived balance rather than base rates.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “The odds have to even out.” (they will, over thousands of events, not tonight)

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re expecting a change because a streak “feels long.”
You confuse long‑run frequency with short‑run probability.
You think the universe owes you a favorable outcome after an unfavorable run.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Humans are pattern‑seeking machines. We misapply the law of large numbers to small samples, expecting local representativeness. The brain also confuses causal “balancing” forces with true randomness.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Explicitly remind yourself: “Each event is independent. The coin/stocks/next client doesn’t know what happened before.”
When gambling, set fixed limits and never chase losses.
In business, evaluate each opportunity on its own merits, not as part of a streak.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking the fallacy means streaks can’t happen; they can and do in random sequences.
Treating genuinely dependent events (like a player’s morale affecting performance) as independent when they aren’t.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A lottery player uses the same numbers for years. After they don’t appear, she switches, convinced the old numbers are “cursed.” The probability of any set of numbers is identical; the past draws don’t affect the future.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Chance has no memory and no sense of fairness. The dice don’t know you’ve been losing, and they don’t care.
